title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 1: On Developing My Decision-Writing Style
keywords: Cruz vs. Correctional Institute for Women
primary_topics: Chapter 1 of 'Justice and Faith' -- CJP's second-anniversary self-account (October 10, 1997) of how he, as a non-career jurist with no prior judicial decision authored, developed his decision-writing style from scratch

Two-year output reckoning -- 230 full-blown signed ponencias, 11 separate opinions, ~140 extended resolutions, ~675 minute resolutions, bound into 11 volumes of ~500 pages each (5,500 pages); ~8.2 pages produced per day including weekends

Style-as-readability thesis -- write in 'simple English comprehensible as much as possible to a high school graduate' so the Constitution is understood by 'ordinary men and women who place their lives on the line in its defense'

Style-as-completeness -- answer and settle all relevant issues raised by the parties, as a corrective to the former-practicing-lawyer's worst nightmare of decisions disposing of cases on one or two issues only

Part I anatomy of CJP's ponencias -- criminal vs. noncriminal cases; six main parts (introduction/prologue → statement of the case → statement of facts → issues/assignment of errors → Court ruling → disposition); with epilogue inserted where new principles or controversial issues require it

Epilogue -- austerity discipline of the chambered jurist: divested all business, civic, professional ties (with three exceptions), bars visitors and personal phone calls, includes all 'personal' letters about Court matters in the Court agenda
sub_topics: Non-career-jurist disclosure -- appointment to the SC was CJP's first full-time government job; he took the oath October 10, 1995, without having authored a single judicial decision
First-decisions chronology -- first dissent (Imelda Marcos v. Comelec) 15 days after oath; first ponencia (Ty v. Trampe) 52 days after, nullifying an unreasonable real-estate-tax increase
Output ledger -- 230 ponencias, 11 separate opinions, ~140 extended resolutions, ~675 minute resolutions; 11 bound volumes of ~500 pages each = 5,500 pages
Per-page averages -- each ponencia averages 25 pages, each opinion 12 pages
Daily-output reckoning -- 8.2 pages per day including Saturdays, Sundays and holidays over 731 days
Caseload baseline -- 'inherited' ~700 pending cases from predecessor + 280 'unloaded' by other incumbents = ~1,000 initial cases; ~35 new cases + ~10 administrative cases per justice per month

Longest/shortest landmarks -- Tañada v. Angara (72 pages, May 2 1997, the WTO case) longest ponencia; Cruz v. Correctional Institute for Women (4 pages, Sept 27 1996) shortest; Echegaray Separate Opinion (32 pages, Feb 7 1997) longest separate opinion; Manila Prince Hotel Dissent (3 pages, Feb 3 1997) shortest
Simple-English thesis -- write to be understood not only by the legal profession but by the parties themselves, especially accused persons, and the public on constitutional cases

Marcos Dissenting Opinion citation -- 'The Constitution is the most basic law of the land... not a document reserved only for scholarly disquisitions... not intended for lawyers to quibble over... Its contents and words should be interpreted in the sense understood by the ordinary men and women who place their lives on the line in its defense and who pin their hopes for a better life on its fulfillment.'

Simplicity-clarity-precision triad -- trend of all professions to be understood by the public at large; no principle so complicated and no mystery so deep that cannot be explained in clear and simple language
Completeness ethic -- strive to state facts as accurately as possible (in the parties' own words if possible) and resolve all issues raised

Progressive-and-cumulative features -- earlier ponencias do not capitalize 'R' in 'Respondent Court' or 'A' in 'Appellant'; topical titles ('Statement of the Case', 'The Case') used more consistently toward the latter part of the two-year period

Style is not literary self-expression -- CJP disclaims any 'distinctive form of prose...as in the style of Mark Twain or of St. Paul'; it is preference of subject presentation, typography, tenses, punctuation, abbreviation, capitalization
No-right-or-wrong-style position -- each justice has his/her own pathway-in-the-mind style; any claim of superiority would be pure hubris

Six main parts of a ponencia -- (1) introduction or prologue, (2) statement of the case, (3) statement of facts, (4) issues or assignment of errors, (5) Court ruling (each issue separately considered and resolved), (6) dispositive portion; with optional epilogue prior to disposition for controversial-issue cases

Criminal cases -- opening either concise statement of principal factual/legal issue, or iteration of a legal maxim, or CJP's own view on the nature and implications of the crime (e.g. People v. Julian 'Rape is chilling, naked sadism')

Statement of the case in criminal cases -- specific charge (information quoted in full); court of origin; judge and date of appealed decision; trial-court criminal case number; plea of accused; dispositive portion of assailed decision

Court's ruling section -- single sentence disposition ('We affirm...' 'The appeal is bereft of merit') then full discussion of each issue numbered 'First Issue', 'Second Issue', sub-topics italicized + underlined + left-justified
Tense convention -- present tense throughout except in statement of facts and rulings of lower courts; drama of each case vivid as if parties are presently arguing

Disposition discipline -- RELEASE-from-confinement clause for acquittals (judgment of acquittal unappealable and immediately executory); proper designation of penalty (prision mayor vs reclusion temporal vs reclusion perpetua vs life imprisonment) because each carries specific accessory penalties

Noncriminal-cases differences -- introduction may include a doctrinal rule, a backgrounder for technical subjects (WTO, local initiative, automotive financing); statement-of-case names which CA/NLRC/Sandiganbayan division and members and ponente; motion for reconsideration mentioned because it is a condition precedent for certiorari
Epilogue -- first two years 'very challenging and engaging,' worked day and night including weekends, never absent or late from any Court session

Austerity-of-chambers -- sold law-firm interests + resigned business + cut professional/civic/religious/charitable memberships (except three); limited social presence to family events, weddings/anniversaries of close friends, golf/tennis with judiciary or pre-appointment friends without known litigations

No-visitors-no-phone-calls rule -- written instructions to SC security; refuses to receive visitors and phone calls; shuns conversation about work; 'personal' letters about Court matters included in Court agenda for proper notation

Three-exception memberships -- Pontifical Council for the Laity (precedent: Feria J.), Rotary Club of Manila (precedents: Malcolm, Paras, Padilla JJ.), Bantayog ng mga Bayani Foundation (precedents: Yap CJ, Sarmiento J.); also Special Minister of Holy Communion in parish (precedent: Vitug J.)

Closing reverence -- 'I cannot close this anniversary piece without thanking our Lord Jesus Christ' -- prayer for wisdom, discernment and courage to do His will; 'Your will be done, oh Lord, not mine'
Constitutional grounding -- Art. VIII Sec. 11 (good behavior until age 70); two-year unloading-old-cases rule for new appointees
signature_phrases: I had to put together and evolve rather speedily my own decision-writing style and format

stances.claim: I am a non-career jurist -- my appointment to the Supreme Court being my first full-time government job -- and I took my oath before President Fidel V. Ramos on October 10, 1995, without having authored a single judicial decision; hence I had to put together and evolve rather speedily my own decision-writing style and format.
stances.rhetorical_move: non-career-jurist disclosure + first-full-time-government-job admission + zero-prior-decision baseline + evolve-rather-speedily methodology framing

stances.claim: Even though my decisions are written primarily to resolve legal issues and are thus emblazoned with a considerable amount of legalese, I have endeavored to write in simple English, comprehensible as much as possible to a high-school graduate -- I want to be understood not only by the legal profession but also by the parties themselves, especially by persons accused of crimes, and by the public at large as regards cases involving interpretation of the Constitution.
stances.rhetorical_move: legalese-conceded-but-overridden-by-simple-English + comprehensible-to-high-school-graduate readability target + four-audience cascade (profession + parties + accused + public)

stances.claim: More than lingual elegance and even legal pugnacity, I strive for simplicity, clarity and precision in nuances and shades of meanings -- no principle is so complicated and no mystery so deep that cannot be explained in clear and simple language to be capable of general understanding.
stances.rhetorical_move: more-than-elegance-or-pugnacity hierarchy + simplicity-clarity-precision triad + nothing-too-complicated-or-too-deep aphorism

stances.claim: As a former practicing lawyer, one of my worst nightmares was to read a decision disposing of a case I argued based merely on one or two of the many issues I raised -- or worse, on issues other than those raised; sometimes courts would narrate facts not backed by the records or the evidence; to avoid these -- now that I am on the backside of the judicial bench -- I strive to state facts as accurately as I can, in the words of the parties if possible, and to resolve all issues raised.
stances.rhetorical_move: former-practicing-lawyer-perspective + worst-nightmare framing + backside-of-the-judicial-bench self-positioning + completeness ethic

stances.claim: Each justice and judge has his/her own style of writing which characterizes pathways in his/her mind; by and large -- except for glaring lapses in grammar, sentence construction, tenses, numbers, or typing -- I believe there is no right or wrong style; any claim of superiority or dominance in writing style by anyone would be pure hubris.
stances.rhetorical_move: pathways-in-the-mind metaphor + no-right-or-wrong-style equanimity + pure-hubris closing rebuke

stances.claim: In discussing and resolving the issues, I use the present tense; in the entirety of the ponencias -- except in the statement of facts and the rulings of the lower courts -- I normally use the present tense; in this manner, the drama of each case becomes more vivid and easier to understand, as if the parties or their counsel are actually and presently arguing, with the Court issuing the corresponding ruling or resolution thereon.

When I joined the Court, I sold completely and absolutely my interests in my law firm, resigned from my business involvements and cut off memberships in professional, civic, religious, charitable and other non-judicial associations, with the exception of three (Pontifical Council for the Laity, Rotary Club of Manila, Bantayog ng mga Bayani Foundation); I refuse to receive visitors and telephone calls, and shun any conversation regarding my work; even letters marked 'personal' I include in the Court's agenda, because there is nothing personal about matters pending before the Court.
stances.rhetorical_move: complete-and-absolute divestment + three-exception roster + no-visitors-no-phone-calls discipline + 'nothing personal' inclusion-in-agenda principle

stances.claim: I cannot close this anniversary piece without thanking our Lord Jesus Christ for the graces and blessings He has mercifully showered me -- in trying to help render justice in our sinful world, my prayer is that I may be granted wisdom, discernment and courage to do His will: 'Your will be done, oh Lord, not mine.'
stances.rhetorical_move: anniversary-piece-closing + thanksgiving + wisdom-discernment-courage triplet + Lord's-Prayer-echo closing

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'Justice and Faith' is CJP's October 10, 1997 second-anniversary self-account of how he, a non-career jurist whose Supreme Court appointment was his first full-time government job, evolved his decision-writing style from zero -- having taken his oath on October 10, 1995 'without having authored a single judicial decision.' He reckons the output: 230 full-blown signed ponencias, 11 separate opinions, ~140 extended resolutions, ~675 minute resolutions, bound into '11 volumes of about 500 pages each or a total of 5,500 pages' -- 8.2 pages per day for 731 days including weekends. His first Dissent (Imelda Marcos v. Comelec, 15 days after oath) and first ponencia (Ty v. Trampe, 52 days after, nullifying an unreasonable real-estate-tax increase) anchor the chronology; Tañada v. Angara (WTO, 72 pages) is the longest ponencia. The thesis: 'simple English comprehensible as much as possible to a high-school graduate' so the Constitution is read 'in the sense understood by the ordinary men and women who place their lives on the line in its defense' (Marcos Dissent). 'More than lingual elegance and even legal pugnacity, I strive for simplicity, clarity and precision in nuances and shades of meanings.' Part I lays out a six-part ponencia anatomy (introduction → statement of the case → statement of facts → issues → Court ruling → disposition, with optional epilogue), distinguishes criminal from noncriminal cases, codifies the present-tense convention ('the drama of each case becomes more vivid... as if the parties or their counsel are actually and presently arguing'), and demands disciplined penalty designation and an acquittal-clause RELEASE language. The Epilogue records the monastic discipline of chambered work -- completely sold his law-firm interests, resigned all business, cut civic memberships with three exceptions (Pontifical Council for the Laity, Rotary Club of Manila, Bantayog ng mga Bayani Foundation), bars visitors and personal phone calls, and includes letters marked 'personal' in the Court agenda because 'there is nothing personal about matters pending before the Court.' He closes with a Lord's-Prayer echo: 'Your will be done, oh Lord, not mine.'
